etymology: Hebrew nephesh chayyah, living soul or living creature; the phrase of Genesis 2:7, when man became a living soul.
biblical_def: Nephesh chayyah is the Hebrew phrase, living soul or living creature, used in the account of creation, and supremely of the making of man: And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul—nephesh chayyah. The phrase is used also of the animals, the living creatures God made; but with man there is a difference the text marks: man alone is formed by God’s own hand from the dust and made alive by the divine in-breathing, and man alone is made in the image of God. Nephesh denotes the living, breathing self, the soul as the principle of life and personhood; chayyah, living. Man became a living soul not by evolving from lower creatures but by the immediate creative act of God, body formed and soul in-breathed—a unity of dust and breath, of body and soul. Paul cites the verse to teach the order of the two Adams: the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit; that which is natural first, then that which is spiritual. The dictionary honors nephesh chayyah as the Scripture’s account of the origin and constitution of man—a living soul made by God, body and spirit united, the crown of creation and the image of his Maker—against every doctrine that would reduce man to a mere animal or deny the special creation and the soul that distinguish him.
webster_summary: Hebrew for living soul; the phrase of Genesis 2:7, when man, formed of dust and given the breath of life, became a living soul—made by God in His image.

corruption_summary: Man is reduced to a mere evolved animal or a soulless body; Scripture confesses man a living soul, specially made by God in His image.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the reductionist account. The chief corruption is the reduction of man to a mere evolved animal, or to a soulless body—a chance arrangement of matter—denying the special creation and the soul that Scripture declares. But Genesis is plain: the LORD God formed man of the dust and breathed into him the breath of life, and man became a living soul (Gen 2:7), made in the image of God (Gen 1:27). Man is not a risen beast but a fallen image-bearer, body formed by God and soul in-breathed by Him.

The principle to recover is the dignity and constitution of man as a living soul made by God. Though the phrase nephesh chayyah is used of the animals too, the text marks man’s difference: he alone is formed by God’s own hand, made alive by the divine in-breathing, and stamped with the image of his Maker. The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life (Job 33:4). And the order of the two Adams crowns the doctrine: the first Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam, Christ, a quickening spirit (1 Cor 15:45), who gives not natural life only but the life everlasting. To confess man a living soul is to honour both his created dignity and his need of the second Adam’s quickening.

etymology: Greek chara, joy; closely kin to charis, grace; the gladness of heart that is the fruit of the Spirit.
biblical_def: Chara is the Greek word for joy, the gladness of heart that is a fruit of the Spirit and a mark of the kingdom of God, which is righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. It is closely kin to charis, grace, for the joy of the believer springs from the grace of God: joy is grace received and rejoiced in. This joy is not the fleeting mirth of the world, which depends on outward circumstance, but a deep and abiding gladness rooted in God and His salvation, which can fill the heart even in tribulation. The Lord told His disciples these things He spoke that His joy might remain in them, and that their joy might be full; the apostles, beaten, departed rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name; Paul, in prison, bids the Philippians Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. The believer is to count it all joy when he falls into divers temptations, and looks unto Jesus, who for the joy that was set before Him endured the cross. The full and final chara is the entering into the joy of the Lord. The dictionary honors chara as the Spirit-given joy of the Christian—not dependent on circumstance but rooted in grace, surviving and even triumphing in suffering, the foretaste of the everlasting gladness of the redeemed in the presence of their Lord, in whose presence is fulness of joy.
webster_summary: Greek for joy, the gladness of heart that is a fruit of the Spirit; kin to grace, rooted in God, abiding even in tribulation, the foretaste of everlasting joy.
webster_full: CHARA, Greek for joy, a fruit of the Spirit.

His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: Joy is reduced to circumstantial happiness or a duty to perform; Scripture knows chara as Spirit-given gladness rooted in grace, abiding even in affliction.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the word joy. The first reduces it to circumstantial happiness—a passing mood that rises and falls with fortune, indistinguishable from the world’s mirth. The second makes it a mere duty to be performed, a forced cheerfulness pasted over an empty heart. Both miss the nature of chara, which is a fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22), grown by God in the soul, not manufactured by man.

The principle to recover is that biblical joy is Spirit-given gladness rooted in the grace of God, which abides and even triumphs in affliction. It is kin to grace itself; the believer’s joy springs from grace received and rejoiced in. The Lord spoke that His joy might remain in His people, and their joy be full (John 15:11); Paul, in prison, could yet command, Rejoice in the Lord alway (Phil 4:4), for this joy does not depend on circumstance but on the Lord. It is no shallow happiness but the deep gladness that counts trials all joy and looks to the everlasting joy beyond—the entering into the joy of the Lord (Matt 25:21). This is the chara the Spirit gives, a foretaste of the fulness of joy in His presence.

etymology: Greek bios, life—the course, means, and manner of natural life; distinguished from zoe, life as such.
biblical_def: Bios is one of the Greek words for life, denoting the course, the means, and the manner of natural life—one’s living, livelihood, and the span and manner of earthly existence—as distinguished from zoe, which denotes life itself, the principle of life, and especially the eternal life that is in Christ. Bios is the word for the substance one lives on: the widow cast into the treasury all her living, all that she had, her whole bios; the prodigal wasted his substance, his bios, in riotous living. It is the word in the warning against the pride of life—the boastful confidence in the goods and pomp of this passing existence, which is not of the Father, but of the world. And it is the word for the means of life that love must share: whoso hath this world’s good, this bios, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? Bios, then, is the believer’s earthly life and goods, given by God, to be held loosely, used faithfully, and surrendered when He calls—not the treasure to be hoarded, but the stewardship to be rendered. The dictionary honors the distinction of bios and zoe as a help to reading the Scriptures: that the believer is not to set his heart on bios, the passing life and its goods, but on zoe, the eternal life that is in the Son, and to use his bios in love and stewardship for the sake of the life that never ends.
webster_summary: Greek for the course and means of natural life—one’s living and livelihood—as distinguished from zoe, life itself; to be held loosely and used in stewardship.
webster_full: BIOS, Greek for the course and means of natural life.

corruption_summary: Earthly life and goods are made the treasure of the heart; Scripture sets bios as the passing life to be held loosely, the heart fixed on the eternal zoe in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the universal instinct of the fallen heart to make bios—the earthly life, its livelihood and goods, its span and comforts—the treasure and the goal, setting the affections on the passing rather than the eternal. Scripture names this the pride of life, which is not of the Father, but of the world (1 John 2:16), and warns that the cares and riches and pleasures of this life choke the word and bring no fruit to perfection (Luke 8:14).

The principle to recover is the distinction between bios and zoe, and the right ordering of the heart. Bios is real and God-given—the believer’s earthly life and means, to be received with thanks and used faithfully—but it is passing, and it is not the treasure. The widow who cast in all her living, her whole bios (Luke 21:4), held it loosely and gave it freely, for her heart was elsewhere. The Christian is to use his bios in love, sharing this world’s good with the brother in need (1 John 3:17), and to set his heart not on bios but on zoe—the eternal life that is in the Son. He holds the passing life with an open hand and clings to the life that never ends.

etymology: Hebrew mitzvot, commandments (singular mitzvah); the precepts of the LORD given in His law.
biblical_def: Mitzvot is the Hebrew word for commandments (the singular is mitzvah), the precepts of the LORD given in His law—the things He has commanded His people to do and to refrain from. The mitzvot are not the arbitrary rules of a tyrant but the good and holy will of a loving God, the revelation of His righteous character and the way of life for His people: the commandment is holy, and just, and good. The psalmist delights in them: O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day; thy commandments are more to be desired than gold, sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. The mitzvot were never given as a ladder by which sinners might climb to God by their own works—for by the deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified—but as the rule of grateful obedience for a people already redeemed: the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt first, and then gave the commandments at Sinai. So for the believer the commandments are not a yoke of bondage but the path of love: If ye love me, keep my commandments; and his commandments are not grievous. The dictionary honors the mitzvot as the holy, good, and loving precepts of the LORD—not a means of earning salvation, which is by grace alone, but the rule of life and the way of love for the redeemed—against both the legalism that would make them a ladder to heaven and the antinomianism that would cast them off as bondage.
webster_summary: Hebrew for commandments, the holy and good precepts of the LORD; not a ladder to earn salvation, but the rule of grateful obedience and love for the redeemed.

corruption_summary: The commandments are made either a ladder to earn salvation or a bondage to be cast off; Scripture holds them holy and good, the rule of love for the redeemed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors corrupt the mitzvot. The first is legalism, which makes the commandments a ladder by which the sinner climbs to God by his own works—against the plain word that by the deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified. The second is antinomianism, which, rejoicing in grace, casts off the commandments as bondage, as though the redeemed had no rule of life. Both pervert the good gift of God’s law.

The principle to recover is the right place of the commandments in the life of grace. The mitzvot are holy, and just, and good (Rom 7:12), the revelation of God’s righteous character and the way of life for His people, in which the psalmist delights: O how love I thy law! (Psa 119:97). They were never given that sinners might earn salvation, but as the rule of grateful obedience for a people already redeemed—the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt before He gave the law at Sinai. So for the believer the commandments are the path of love, not the price of acceptance: If ye love me, keep my commandments (John 14:15), and His commandments are not grievous (1 John 5:3). Saved by grace, the redeemed keep the mitzvot out of love, not to be saved but because they are.

etymology: Latin fiducia, trust, confidence; the element of saving faith that is personal trust in Christ, beyond knowledge and assent.
biblical_def: Fiducia is the Latin word for trust or confidence, used by the Reformed theologians for the third and crowning element of saving faith. The divines distinguished three elements in faith: notitia, knowledge of the truth of the gospel; assensus, assent that this truth is indeed true; and fiducia, the personal trust by which the soul rests upon and receives Christ Himself for salvation. The devils have notitia and assensus—they know and believe that there is one God, and tremble—but they have no fiducia, no trusting of themselves to Christ. Saving faith is not mere knowledge, nor bare assent to facts, but the actual leaning of the whole soul upon Christ, the receiving and resting upon Him alone for salvation, as He is offered in the gospel. It is the faith that says, I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him—a committing, a trusting, a casting of oneself wholly on the Saviour. This fiducia is itself the gift of God, wrought in the heart by the Spirit. The dictionary honors fiducia as the heart of saving faith—the personal trust that rests upon Christ alone, beyond mere knowledge and assent—against the dead faith that knows and assents but never trusts, and presses upon every hearer that to be saved is not merely to believe the gospel is true, but to cast oneself, in trust, wholly upon the Christ it reveals.
webster_summary: Latin for trust; the crowning element of saving faith—personal trust resting on Christ alone—beyond knowledge (notitia) and assent (assensus), which even devils have.

corruption_summary: Faith is reduced to mere knowledge or assent to facts; Scripture and the Reformed know saving faith as fiducia, the personal trust that rests on Christ alone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the reduction of saving faith to mere knowledge or bare assent—believing the facts of the gospel to be true, while never trusting oneself to the Christ those facts reveal. James exposes this dead faith: the devils also believe that there is one God, and tremble (Jas 2:19); they have notitia and assensus in full, yet are not saved, for they have no fiducia. A faith that knows and assents but never trusts is the faith of demons, not of saints.

The principle to recover is that the heart of saving faith is fiducia, personal trust resting on Christ alone. Beyond knowing the gospel and assenting to it, the soul must lean its whole weight upon Christ, receiving and resting upon Him as He is offered. This is the faith that receives Him (John 1:12), that puts its trust in Him (Psa 2:12), that can say with Paul, I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that He is able to keep that which I have committed unto Him (2 Tim 1:12)—a committing of the soul to the Saviour. Such trust is itself the gift of God, wrought by the Spirit. To be saved is therefore not merely to believe the gospel true, but to cast oneself, in trust, wholly upon the Christ it reveals.

etymology: From 1 Peter 1:13; the figure of girding up the mind for ready, disciplined action, drawn from girding the loins.
biblical_def: Loins of the mind is the figure used by Peter in his charge to the scattered saints: Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. In the East, a man wearing the long, flowing robe would gather it up and tuck it into his girdle when he meant to run, to work, or to fight, so that the loose garment would not hinder him; to gird up the loins was to make ready for vigorous action. So to gird up the loins of the mind is to gather in the loose and wandering thoughts, to brace and discipline the mind for the work and warfare of the Christian life, to put away the slackness and dissipation that hinder, and to set the whole mind in readiness for service and for the hope of Christ’s appearing. It is a summons to mental discipline and sober earnestness, the opposite of a careless, distracted, undisciplined mind. The same figure underlies the Lord’s command, Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning, like servants waiting for their lord. The dictionary honors the phrase loins of the mind as a call to disciplined, sober, ready-minded Christian living—to gather in the wandering thoughts, brace the mind for duty and for warfare, and live in earnest readiness for the coming of the Lord—against the slack, distracted, dissipated mind that the present age so loves.
webster_summary: Peter’s figure (1 Pet 1:13) for bracing and disciplining the mind for ready action, as a man girds up his robe to run; a call to sober, watchful earnestness.

corruption_summary: The mind is left slack, distracted, and undisciplined; Scripture calls the believer to gird up the loins of the mind for sober, ready, watchful service.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the slack, distracted, dissipated mind that the present age so loves and cultivates—a mind of scattered attention, endless amusement, and undisciplined thought, the very opposite of what Peter commands. To leave the mind ungirded, its thoughts loose and trailing like an unbelted robe, is to be hindered at every step in the work and warfare of the Christian life.

The principle to recover is the call to mental discipline and sober readiness. Gird up the loins of your mind, be sober (1 Pet 1:13): gather in the wandering thoughts, brace the mind, put away dissipation, and set the whole understanding in readiness for duty and for the hope of Christ’s appearing. The same figure runs through Scripture: let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning, like servants watching for their lord (Luke 12:35); stand having your loins girt about with truth (Eph 6:14); be men in understanding (1 Cor 14:20). The believer is to live with a disciplined, earnest, watchful mind, ready for service and for the coming of the Lord—not careless and distracted, but girded and alert.

pronunciation: thuh HID-uhn man uhv thuh hart
etymology: From 1 Peter 3:4; the inward, spiritual self, the true adorning of the believer, especially the godly woman.
biblical_def: The hidden man of the heart is Peter’s phrase for the inward, spiritual self—the true and abiding character of the soul as opposed to the outward, visible adorning of the body. Charging Christian wives, the apostle writes that their adorning should not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The hidden man of the heart is the renewed inner self, the new creature, whose true beauty is invisible to the eye but precious to God. Its ornament is not gold or fine clothing, which perish, but the incorruptible graces of the Spirit—a meek and quiet spirit, of great price in His sight. The principle is not that outward neatness is forbidden, but that the heart, not the body, is the seat of true and lasting beauty, and that the believer—and especially the godly woman—is to give chief care to the adorning of the inner self. The dictionary honors the hidden man of the heart as the Scripture’s account of true beauty—the renewed inner self, adorned with the incorruptible ornament of a meek and quiet spirit—against an age obsessed with the corruptible adorning of the outward body, and presses the godly to seek that beauty which is in the sight of God of great price.
webster_summary: Peter’s phrase for the inward spiritual self, the believer’s true adorning; its ornament a meek and quiet spirit, incorruptible, in God’s sight of great price.
webster_full: HIDDEN MAN OF THE HEART, the inward spiritual self (1Pe 3:4).

corruption_summary: True worth is sought in outward appearance and adornment; Scripture sets the hidden man of the heart, adorned with a meek and quiet spirit, as the beauty of great price.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the cult of the outward. The corruption is the obsession, ancient and modern, with the outward adorning—seeking worth, identity, and beauty in the appearance of the body, the hair, the apparel, the corruptible things that perish. An age that lavishes endless care on the outward man and neglects the inner has inverted the values of Scripture, which prizes what God prizes: not the visible, but the hidden man of the heart.

The principle to recover is that true and lasting beauty is inward and spiritual. Peter directs the godly woman’s adorning not to the outward plaiting of hair and wearing of gold (1 Pet 3:3), but to the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price (1 Pet 3:4). For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7). The outward man perishes, but the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). This is no forbidding of neatness, but a reordering of the heart’s care: to seek above all the incorruptible beauty of the renewed inner self, precious in the sight of God.

etymology: From Hebrews 9:14; the cleansing of the conscience from dead works by the blood of Christ.
biblical_def: Purge the conscience is the phrase of Hebrews for the cleansing of the inner man—the conscience defiled by sin—by the blood of Christ, that the worshipper may serve the living God with a clear and peaceful heart. The writer contrasts the old sacrifices with the new: the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctified to the purifying of the flesh—an outward, ceremonial cleansing only; how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? The old sacrifices could not make the comers thereunto perfect as pertaining to the conscience; they were a yearly remembrance of sins, but could not take them away or cleanse the guilty heart. Only the blood of Christ reaches the conscience itself, removing the guilt and defilement that the law could only cover, so that the believer may draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience. To have the conscience purged is to be freed from the accusing, condemning sense of guilt before God, washed not outwardly but inwardly by the blood of the Lamb. The dictionary honors this phrase as a precious fruit of the atonement—that Christ’s blood cleanses not the flesh only but the conscience, removing guilt and giving peace—against every religion of outward ceremony that leaves the inner man defiled, and presses the burdened soul to the blood that alone can purge it.
webster_summary: The cleansing of the conscience from the guilt of dead works by the blood of Christ; what the old sacrifices could not reach, His blood removes, giving the heart peace.

corruption_summary: Religion is reduced to outward ceremony that leaves the conscience defiled; Scripture proclaims Christ’s blood alone purges the conscience from guilt, giving peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the religion of outward ceremony—rites, washings, penances, and observances—that touches only the flesh and leaves the inner man defiled, the conscience still accusing and unclean. The old covenant sacrifices themselves could do no more: the blood of bulls and goats sanctified to the purifying of the flesh (Heb 9:13), but could not make the worshipper perfect as pertaining to the conscience, nor take away the consciousness of sin (Heb 10:2). Every merely external religion shares this impotence.

The principle to recover is that the blood of Christ alone purges the conscience. How much more shall the blood of Christ, who offered Himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? (Heb 9:14). His blood reaches what the law could not—the inner man, the guilty conscience itself—removing not the outward stain only but the inward guilt, so that the believer may draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience (Heb 10:22). This is the peace the burdened soul seeks and cannot find in ceremony: the cleansing of the conscience by the blood of the Lamb, which frees from the accusing weight of guilt and sets the heart at liberty to serve the living God.

etymology: From Romans 12:1; the charge to offer the whole self to God as a living sacrifice.
biblical_def: Present yourselves is the apostle Paul’s charge at the turning-point of Romans, where, having set forth the mercies of God through eleven chapters of doctrine, he turns to exhortation: I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. The word present is the language of the altar—to offer, to yield up—but the sacrifice is not a slain beast but the believer’s own self, a living sacrifice, the whole man given over to God for His service. It is grounded wholly in grace: by the mercies of God—the response of gratitude for all that the gospel has freely given, not a price to earn it. Paul presses the same word elsewhere: yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. To present oneself is to make a deliberate, total, and reasonable surrender of body and soul to the Lord who bought it—reasonable, for it is the only fitting response to such mercy. It is followed at once by the call not to be conformed to this world, but to be transformed by the renewing of the mind. The dictionary honors this charge as the gateway of the consecrated life: that the believer, moved by the mercies of God, yields his whole self a living sacrifice to God—the reasonable, grateful, and total surrender that is the beginning of true holiness.

corruption_summary: Consecration is made a means to earn God’s favor, or reduced to partial, occasional surrender; Scripture grounds it in grace and calls for the whole self offered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the charge to present oneself. The first makes consecration a means to earn God’s favor—a sacrifice offered to buy His acceptance—reversing the gospel order. The second reduces it to a partial, occasional surrender, yielding a corner of life while keeping the rest. But Paul’s charge is grounded in grace and demands the whole: by the mercies of God, present your bodies a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1)—the response of gratitude for mercy already received, and the offering not of a part but of the whole self.

The principle to recover is the grateful, total, reasonable surrender of the self to God. The motive is mercy: only after eleven chapters setting forth the riches of grace does Paul say, I beseech you therefore, by the mercies of God. The offering is the whole man, a living sacrifice; the manner is deliberate and complete, as the Macedonians first gave their own selves to the Lord (2 Cor 8:5); the fruit is transformation, not conformity to the world (Rom 12:2). To present oneself is the gateway of the consecrated life: yielding body and soul to the Lord who bought them, as those that are alive from the dead (Rom 6:13)—the reasonable service that is the beginning of true holiness, flowing not from fear or merit but from grateful love.

etymology: From Revelation 2:17 and Isaiah 62:2; the new name given by God to His redeemed, a token of new and accepted identity.
biblical_def: The new name is the new designation God gives to His redeemed, a token of a new, accepted, and intimate identity bestowed by grace. To him that overcometh, the Lord promises, will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it. Isaiah foretold it of restored Zion: thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the LORD shall name; and again, thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken, but thou shalt be called Hephzibah—my delight is in her. Throughout Scripture God marks a new beginning by a new name: Abram became Abraham, Sarai Sarah, Jacob Israel, Simon Peter—the new name signifying a new calling, a new covenant standing, a new character given by God. The new name promised to the overcomer speaks of the believer’s secret and intimate acceptance with God, a name known to him alone in the depths of communion, a token that he is owned, accepted, and beloved. It points to the consummation, when the redeemed shall bear the name of God and of the Lamb in their foreheads, fully His for ever. The dictionary honors the new name as a precious emblem of the believer’s new identity in Christ—owned, renamed, and accepted by sovereign grace—against the false identities the world bestows, and as a pledge of the intimate, everlasting acceptance the redeemed shall know in the presence of their God.

corruption_summary: Identity is sought in self-made or world-given names; Scripture gives the new name by grace, a token of acceptance God Himself bestows on His redeemed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the cult of self-made identity. The corruption is the modern quest to name oneself—to forge one’s own identity by self-assertion, or to receive it from the shifting names the world bestows. But the new name of Scripture is given, not seized; it is named by the mouth of the LORD (Isa 62:2), written by God upon His redeemed. True identity is not self-created but grace-given; the soul does not name itself but is named by its Maker and Redeemer.

The principle to recover is that the believer’s new identity is the gift of God, a token of acceptance He Himself bestows. God has ever marked new beginnings by new names—Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel, Simon to Peter—each signifying a new calling and covenant standing. To the overcomer He promises a white stone, and a new name written, which no man knoweth but he that receiveth it (Rev 2:17): a name of secret, intimate acceptance, known in the depths of communion with God. He writes upon His own His new name and the name of the city of God (Rev 3:12), and calls the once-forsaken Hephzibah, my delight is in her, for the LORD delighteth in her (Isa 62:4). The new name is the pledge that the redeemed are owned, accepted, and beloved—named by grace, and His for ever.
